text:
CYRANO:
  Why!
  I had taken it upon myself: I was interpreting thy passion!
  Sometimes I wrote without telling thee: I am writing!

CHRISTIAN:
  Ah?

CYRANO:
  It is quite simple!

CHRISTIAN:
  But how didst thou manage,
  Since we have been blockaded, to?...

CYRANO:
  Oh!...before dawn
  I could cross over...

CHRISTIAN (folding his arms):
  Ah! it is quite simple again?
  And how many times a week did I write?...Twice?—Three times?—
  Four?—

CYRANO:
  More.

CHRISTIAN:
  Every day?

CYRANO:
  Yes, every day.—Twice.

CHRISTIAN (violently):
  And that intoxicated thee, and the intoxication was such
  That thou didst brave death...

CYRANO (seeing Roxane returning):
  Be silent! Not before her!
  (He quickly goes back into his tent.)



Scene 4.VIII.

Roxane, Christian; in the background, cadets coming and going. Carbon and De
Guiche give orders.


ROXANE (running to Christian):
  And now, Christian!...

CHRISTIAN (taking her hands):
  And now, tell me
  Why, by these dreadful roads, why
  Through all these ranks of soldiers and troopers,
  Thou hast joined me here?

ROXANE:
  It is because of the letters!

CHRISTIAN:
  What dost thou say?

ROXANE:
  So much the worse for you if I run these dangers!
  It is your letters that have intoxicated me! Ah! consider
  How many you have written me for the past month,
  And always more beautiful!

CHRISTIAN:
  What! For a few little
  Love letters...

ROXANE:
  Be silent! Thou canst not know!
  My God, I adored thee, it is true, from the night when,
  In a voice I had not known was thine, beneath my window,
  Thy soul began to make itself known...
  Well! Thy letters, thou seest, for the past month,
  Are as though all the while I heard it, thy voice
  From that night, so tender, and which enfolds you!
  So much the worse for thee, I hasten here. The wise Penelope
  Would not have remained beneath her roof embroidering,
  Had Lord Ulysses written as thou dost,
  But, to join him, as mad as Helen,
  She too would have sent her balls of wool packing!...

CHRISTIAN:
  But...

ROXANE:
  I read, I read again, I swooned,
  I was thine. Each of those little sheets
  Was like a petal blown from thy soul.
  In every word of those letters of flame one feels
  Love, powerful, sincere...

CHRISTIAN:
  Ah! Sincere and powerful?
  It can be felt, Roxane?...

ROXANE:
  Oh! How it can be felt!

CHRISTIAN:
  And you come?...

ROXANE:
  I come (O my Christian, my master!
  You would raise me if I wished to kneel
  At your feet, so it is my soul I lay there,
  And you will never be able to raise it again!)
  I come to ask thy forgiveness (and it is indeed the hour
  To ask forgiveness, since we may die!)
  For having at first, in my frivolity,
  Insulted thee by loving thee for thy beauty alone!

CHRISTIAN (in terror):
  Ah! Roxane!

ROXANE:
  And later, my friend, less frivolous,
  —A bird that hops before it fully takes flight,—
  Thy beauty holding me, thy soul drawing me onward,
  I loved thee for the two together!...

CHRISTIAN:
  And now?

ROXANE:
  Well! At last thy true self triumphs over thyself,
  And it is now for thy soul alone that I love thee!

CHRISTIAN (drawing back):
  Ah! Roxane!

ROXANE:
  Then be happy. For to be loved
  Only for that in which one is costumed for a moment
  Must torture an eager and noble heart;
  But thy dear mind effaces thy face,
  And the beauty by which at first thou didst please me,
  Now I see more clearly...and I no longer see it!

CHRISTIAN:
  Oh!...

ROXANE:
  Dost thou still doubt such a victory?...

CHRISTIAN (painfully):
  Roxane!

ROXANE:
  I understand, thou canst not believe
  In this love?...

CHRISTIAN:
  I do not want this love!
  I want to be loved more simply for...

ROXANE:
  For
  What women have loved in you until this hour?
  Then let yourself be loved in a better way!

CHRISTIAN:
  No! It was better before!

ROXANE:
  Ah! Thou understandest nothing about it!
  It is now that I love more, that I love rightly!
  It is that which makes thee thyself, dost thou hear, that I adore!
  And less handsome...

CHRISTIAN:
  Be silent!

ROXANE:
  I would love thee still!
  If all thy beauty suddenly flew away...

CHRISTIAN:
  Oh! Do not say that!

ROXANE:
  Yes, I say it!

CHRISTIAN:
  What? Ugly?

ROXANE:
  Ugly! I swear it!

CHRISTIAN:
  God!

ROXANE:
  And is thy joy profound?

CHRISTIAN (in a stifled voice):
  Yes...

ROXANE:
  What is the matter with thee?

CHRISTIAN (gently pushing her away):
  Nothing. Two words to say: one second...

ROXANE:
  But?...

CHRISTIAN (showing her a group of cadets in the background):
  My love took thee away from those poor fellows:
  Go and smile upon them a little, since they are going to die...go!

ROXANE (moved):
  Dear Christian!...
  (She goes upstage toward the Gascons, who respectfully crowd around
  her.)



Scene 4.IX.

Christian, Cyrano; in the background, Roxane talking with Carbon and a few cadets.


CHRISTIAN (calling toward Cyrano's tent):
  Cyrano?

CYRANO (reappearing, armed for battle):
  What is it? Thou art pale!

CHRISTIAN:
  She no longer loves me!

CYRANO:
  What?

CHRISTIAN:
  It is thee she loves!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  She loves nothing but my soul now!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  Yes!
  So it is indeed thee she loves—and thou lovest her too!

CYRANO:
  I?

CHRISTIAN:
  I know it.

CYRANO:
  It is true.

CHRISTIAN:
  Like a madman.

CYRANO:
  More.

CHRISTIAN:
  Tell her!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  Why?

CYRANO:
  Look at my face!

CHRISTIAN:
  She would love me ugly!

CYRANO:
  She told thee so!

CHRISTIAN:
  There!

CYRANO:
  Ah! I am very glad she told thee that!
  But come, come, do not believe such a mad thing!
  —My God, I am glad she thought
  To say it—but come, do not take her at her word;
  Come, do not become ugly: she would resent me too much for it!

CHRISTIAN:
  That is what I want to see!

CYRANO:
  No, no!

CHRISTIAN:
  Let her choose!
  Thou art going to tell her everything!
